A novel microbubbles-assisted Fe-C micro-electrolysis system to bridge the 
anaerobic digestion and microalgae cultivation: the dual drive of electron 
transfer and coagulation
Xiaogang You a,b, Libin Yang a,b,*, Mingchao Yang a,b, Jiaying Ma a,b, Futao Yi a,b,  
Tongcai Liu a,b, Bo-Yu Peng a,b, Jiabin Chen a,b, Huaqiang Chu a,b, Buchun Si c,d, Xuefei Zhou a,b,*,  
Yalei Zhang a,b
a State Key Laboratory of Water Pollution Control and Green Resource Recycling, Shanghai 200092, China
b College of Environmental Science and Engineering, Tongji University, Shanghai 200092, China
c College of Water Resources and Civil Engineering, China Agricultural University, Beijing 100083, China
d Department of Agricultural & Biological Engineering, University of Illinois at Urbana-Champaign, Urbana 61801, USA
A R T I C L E  I N F O
Keywords:
Biogas slurry
Microbubbles
Fe-C pretreatment
Oxidation
Self-accelerating coagulation
Microalgae activity
A B S T R A C T
Microalgae-based biogas slurry treatment systems, which possess the dual capability of assimilating nutrients and 
sequestering CO2, are widely recognized as a promising technology. However, the complex composition of biogas 
slurry hinders microalgal metabolic activity and limits the system’s efficiency. In this study, a novel 
microbubbles-assisted Fe-C micro-electrolysis (MFC) system was proposed for biogas slurry pretreatment to 
overcome the bottleneck of utilizing microalgae in biogas slurry treatment. The MFC system significantly 
improved the electron transfer rate, which facilitated the oxidation of Fe(II) to Fe(III) and achieved self- 
accelerating coagulation, increasing the removal efficiencies of dissolved organic matter (DOM) and turbidity 
to 37.3% and 94.9%, respectively. The results revealed that rapid oxidation and continuous perturbation by 
microbubbles caused the formation of more single-corner coordination between FeO6 octahedrons, as well as 
inhibited the transformation of hydrotalcite to the highly crystalline mineral. The accumulation of hydrotalcite 
significantly enhances the adsorption of specific types of DOM by forming a more stable structure in the flocs. In 
addition, the MFC system effectively removed stressors (e.g., humic-like substances, aromatic compounds, and 
residual iron ions) of microalgae in biogas slurry and increased the maximum quantum conversion efficiency 
(Fv/Fm) of the photosynthetic system from 0.455 to 0.556. Consequently, the biomass of microalgae cultured in 
the biogas slurry treated by the MFC system was increased by 42.7% compared to the conventional Fe-C micro- 
electrolysis (CFC) system. Overall, this study demonstrates that MFC-driven oxidative synergistic self- 
accelerating coagulation is a promising process for the stabilization and sustainability of microalgae-based 
biogas slurry treatment.
1. Introduction
Biogas slurry, a byproduct of anaerobic digestion, is rich in organic 
compounds and nutrients, which pose potential threats to the ecosystem 
if not managed properly [13]. In China, the discharge of biogas slurry is 
substantial due to the widespread adoption of anaerobic digestion for 
farm wastewater treatment. Among them, the swine wastewater 
discharge has escalated to 228.3 million with an assumed volume of 
5.26 t wastewater/pig [31]. The residual biogas slurry remains a source 
of environmental concern due to its high content of bioavailable nutri­
ents, including nitrogen and phosphorus. Common methods of biogas 
slurry treatment include artificial wetlands [14], membrane filtration 
[38], struvite crystallization [7], and aerobic treatment. However, these 
methods still face limitations such as low efficiency, high cost, poor 
scalability, or high energy consumption in practical applications.
The integration of microalgae cultivation with biogas slurry treat­
ment presents a sustainable system for recycling nutrients from biogas 
slurry. Moreover, it offers numerous additional advantages, including

nutrient recovery, carbon sequestration, and value-added biomass pro­
duction [2,36]. However, the complex composition of biogas slurries 
may include animal manure, food waste, and agricultural residues, all of 
which can impact microalgae cultivation [13]. For instance, agricultural 
residues contain lignocellulose, which contributes to high turbidity and 
is difficult to degrade. Food waste may introduce additives such as heavy 
metals and antibiotics, while animal manure typically contains elevated 
levels of ammonia nitrogen.
Before microalgae cultivation, pretreatment is typically employed to 
reduce inhibitory factors in biogas slurry. For instance, centrifugation 
effectively removes suspended solids and colloidal particles, thereby 
reducing the turbidity of biogas slurry. However, its high energy con­
sumption limits its scalability for large-scale applications [36]. Filtration 
offers a low-energy alternative, but filter clogging and frequent main­
tenance remain challenges [38]. Other methods, such as flocculation, 
dilution, and advanced oxidation processes, also require balancing ef­
ficiency and operational costs [1,32]. Hence, there is an urgent need for 
an advanced pretreatment technology with engineering potential.
Fe-C particles have been widely used in wastewater treatment owing 
to their simplicity, cost-effectiveness, and sustainability [11,20]. The Fe- 
C micro-electrolysis accompanied by oxidation, reduction, adsorption, 
and coagulation, shows enormous potential in the removal of harmful 
pollutants (e.g., heavy metals, polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbons, humic 
acids, etc.) from biogas slurry [15]. Nevertheless, the low mass transfer 
efficiency and narrow pH range of conventional Fe-C micro-electrolysis 
limit the electron transfer rate, making the removal of pollutants un­
satisfactory [15,39]. These issues directly impede the system’s ability to 
pretreat biogas slurry effectively for microalgae cultivation. While en­
hancements like the addition of chemicals [10], magnetic fields [39], 
and structural improvements [29]have been attempted, the operational 
complexity and scalability limitations make these methods impractical 
for large-scale applications.
In addition, the turbidity of the biogas slurry can be effectively 
removed by coagulation, which is essential for microalgae cultivation. 
However, there are few studies on the coagulation enhancement 
mechanism of Fe-C micro-electrolysis. Fe(III) produced by the oxidation 
of Fe(II) can lead to the precipitation of colloidal-sized (0.02–0.2 μm) Fe 
(hydr)oxides, like ferrihydrite [26]. Ferrihydrite can adsorb organic 
functional groups in the biogas slurry and subsequently aggregate to 
form sinking authigenic particulate Fe, due to its high reactivity and 
expansive specific surface area [24]. However, the Fe-C micro-elec­
trolysis system tends to be acidic, thus lowering the oxidation rate of Fe 
(II) [39]. Furthermore, ferrihydrite is a poorly crystalline mineral and 
undergoes a gradual transformation into highly crystalline minerals, 
compromising their capacity for adsorption and coagulation perfor­
mance of pollutants [30]. Hence, further investigation is needed to 
enhance the rate of Fe-C micro-electrolysis and improve the coagulation 
performance for pollutant removal of the biogas slurry.
Recently, microbubbles (with diameters < 100 μm), with high mass 
transfer efficiency and robust interface effect, have gained extensive 
application in wastewater treatment [23]. These properties have the 
potential to accelerate the rate of electron transfer in Fe-C micro-elec­
trolysis processes. Microbubbles-assisted aeration has also been reported 
to be advantageous in reducing energy consumption and costs [8]. 
Additionally, previous studies have found that a substantial quantity of 
hydroxyl radicals (•OH) are generated during the collapse of micro­
bubbles [9], which can accelerate both pollutant degradation and the 
oxidation of Fe(II) to Fe(III). In situ formation of Fe(III) species by 
oxidizing Fe(II) is typically more effective in water treatment compared 
to the direct addition of Fe(III) [33]. These studies indicate the potential 
contribution of microbubbles to the efficiency of conventional Fe-C 
micro-electrolysis treatment of biogas slurry.
To address the dual challenges of sluggish electron transfer and 
incomplete coagulation in conventional Fe-C systems, this study pro­
poses a novel microbubbles-assisted Fe-C micro-electrolysis (MFC) sys­
tem. The MFC was applied to biogas slurry pretreatment to make it more 
suitable for microalgae cultivation. Specifically, the performance of 
removing pollutants and different types of dissolved organic matter 
(DOM) by degradation and coagulation was evaluated. Additionally, the 
mechanism related to the microbubbles enhancing the electron transfer 
rate of micro-electrolysis was illustrated. Furthermore, the effect of 
microbubbles on the coordination structure of Fe atoms and the crucial 
role of various Fe minerals transformations in the coagulation process 
for DOM removal were analyzed. Finally, the improvement of micro­
algae culture performance by pretreated biogas slurry and the feasibility 
of nutrient utilization were investigated. Overall, the proposed process 
can effectively improve the stabilization and sustainability of 
microalgae-based biogas slurry treatment systems, demonstrating great 
potential for supporting the transition to sustainable water treatment.
2. Materials and methods
2.1. Raw materials and swine biogas slurry
Fe-C particles (3–6 mm in diameter) were obtained from Green 
Source Activated Carbon Co., Ltd. China. The characterization details 
are given in Text S1 and Fig. S1. Microbubbles with a mean size of 31.16 
± 1.32 μm and a concentration of 1.63 × 106 bubbles/mL (Fig. S2), were 
generated by a microbubble generator (ZJC-NM-200L, Zhongjing, 
China). Conventional bubbles with an average size of about 1 mm, were 
produced using a commercially available cylindrical bubble stone 
aeration.
Swine biogas slurry was collected from the anaerobic digester 
effluent of a swine farm in Jinshan, Shanghai, China. To minimize the 
impact of particulate matter in the biogas slurry on experimental errors, 
the slurry was filtered using medium-speed filter paper to remove most 
particulate solids. The processed slurry was then stored at 4 ◦C for 
subsequent use. The characteristics of the row biogas slurry (RBS) are 
shown in Table S1.
2.2. Experimental design
Biogas slurry pretreatment experiments (Fig. 1) were conducted 
using a 500 mL reactor in which the RBS was adjusted to pH = 5 and 
treated under different conditions. Two systems were spiked with 50 g/L 
of Fe-C particles, and the air was passed (50 mL/min) in the form of 
microbubbles and conventional bubbles, which were recorded as MFC 
and CFC, respectively. Another system without Fe-C particles was fed 
only with air microbubbles (50 mL/min), recorded as MBs. All systems 
were maintained at room temperature (25 ◦C) for 2 h, and samples were 
taken at regular intervals during the reaction for analysis.
The treated biogas slurry was used to culture microalgae to explore 
improvements in microalgae growth. The microalgae (Chlorella pyr­
enoidosa, FACHB-9) was consistent with previous study [25]. To opti­
mize microalgae cultivation, the processed biogas slurry was 
appropriately diluted and supplemented with phosphorus after pre­
treatment. Detailed information is presented in Text S2.
2.3. Analytical methods
2.3.1. Determination of biogas slurry water quality
The analytical methods of water quality are illustrated in the Text S3. 
3D excitation −
emission matrix (EEM) spectrofluorometry (Text S4) 
and two-dimensional correlation spectroscopy of UV (UV 2D-COS) (Text 
S5) were used to characterize the fluorescent and UV-active compo­
nents, respectively. Several optical parameters were calculated from the 
EEM and UV −visible spectral data are outlined in Table S2. A principal 
component analysis (PCA) was conducted using the Origin 2021.
2.3.2. Characterization of Fe-C micro-electrolysis rate
The Fe-C particles after the reaction were collected and then washed 
with deionized water. After vacuum freeze-drying, surface samples of

characterized (Text S6). The electrochemical properties of the Fe-C 
particles were measured using a three-electrode cell (CHI760E, CH In­
struments, China). Details of the electrode preparation methods and 
tests are given in Text S7.
2.3.3. Determination of active species
Fe (IV) was detected by the sulfoxide probe method [19]. The 
amount of •OH is determined by terephthalic acid photoluminescence 
(TA-PL) probing means. The detailed methodology is in Text S8.
2.3.4. Characterization of floc samples
Floc samples were centrifuged (3000 rpm, 2 min) and freeze-dried to 
obtain a powdered solid. The surface functional groups and elemental 
composition analysis of floc samples can be found in Text S9. 
Synchrotron radiation-based Fourier transform infrared (SR-FTIR) ob­
tained at the beamline BL01B1 of the National Facility for Protein Sci­
ence in Shanghai (NFPS) was used to analyze differences in the 
distribution of different functional groups, the details are given in Text 
S10. Extended x-ray absorption fine structure (EXAFS) of the coordi­
nation environment of Fe within flocs was analyzed by bulk Fe K-edge 
(7112 eV) on beamline BL14W1 of the NFPS, the details are shown in 
Text S11.
2.3.5. Determination of microalgae growth and cell activity
The microalgae biomass concentrations were determined by optical 
density measurements at a wavelength of 680 nm [25]. Microalgae 
cultured for 3 days were taken to measure the intracellular oxidative 
stress activity [35]. Details of the methodology are in Text S12. The 
fluorescence of the microalgae was measured using a chlorophyll

2.4. Statistical analysis
All data were evaluated with IBM SPSS statistics 25.0 software using 
ANOVA to compare the data of each system for significant change (95 % 
confidence interval). Significant difference was identified at the levels of 
p < 0.05.
3. Results and discussion
3.1. Effects of degradation and coagulation on water quality
The optimization of microbubbles-assisted pretreatment perfor­
mance was evaluated by varying water quality characteristics in 
different systems. The total organic carbon (TOC) concentration 
(Fig. 2a) in the MFC system decreased drastically within the initial 20 
min and continued to decrease moderately from the 20th to the 120th 
minute. The MFC system presented the highest TOC removal efficiency 
(37.3 %), followed by the CFC system (27.7 %) and the MBs system 
(15.3 %). The variation in UV254 (Fig. S3a) was similar to TOC con­
centration changes across all systems. These findings imply that the 
DOM elimination ability was notably promoted with the assistance of 
microbubbles. Microbubbles can generate a larger Laplace pressure and 
exhibit extended retention time in the water, allowing them to increase 
the O2 transfer rate [8]. Consequently, we observed a significant in­
crease in dissolved oxygen (DO) concentration (Fig. 2b) in the MFC and 
MBs systems. As an electron acceptor, O2 can increase the cathodic 
reduction reaction potential, and its increased concentration can 
accelerate electron transfer and DOM degradation [39]. Additionally, 
the production of •OH by the collapse of microbubbles [9]may 
contribute to the degradation of DOM [8].
The Fe (hydr)oxides generated by the iron electrode reaction can 
further remove DOM and suspended particulate matter by adsorption 
and coagulation [33]. This can be verified by the substantial flocs 
formed in the MFC and CFC systems (Fig. S4). Compared with the CFC 
system (61.2 %), the turbidity (Fig. 2c) removal efficiencies were 
improved by 55.0 % in the MFC system (94.9 %), indicating that 
coagulation and settling properties of particulate matter with Fe (hydr) 
oxides were facilitated by the microbubbles. The variation in TN, NH4
+- 
N, and PO4
3--P concentration is illustrated in Fig. S3. PO4
3--P was rendered 
undetectable in the MFC and CFC systems after the operation due to the 
formation of Fe3(PO4)2 and FePO4 precipitates [33]. Detailed discussion 
about the effects of different systems on TN, NH4
+-N, and PO4
3--P removal 
is available in Text S13.
3.2. Specific types of DOM elimination analysis
The components of DOM in the biogas slurry are complex, and 
different components exert distinct effects on biochemical and micro­
algae activities. Different DOM removal efficiencies in various systems 
were further explored. The fluorescence properties of DOM changed 
substantially after treatment (Fig. S5). The total fluorescence (TF) of 
DOM decreased to 28.2 %, 32.9 %, and 52.5 % of RBS in the MFC, CFC, 
and MBs systems, respectively (Fig. 2d). The parallel factor (PARAFAC) 
analysis identified two independent fluorescence components: humic- 
like (C1) and protein-like (C2) substances (Fig. S6 and Table S6). The 
MFC system exhibited escalated removal of both components (Fig. 2d). 
Notably, C1 demonstrated a higher removal rate compared to C2, sug­
gesting it is more easily dominated in electron competition [18]. Fluo­
rescence regional integration (FRI) results also showed that the C1 
component (Region V) in the MFC and CFC systems is lower than that in 
the MBs system (Fig. S8). Previous studies have reported that C1 can be 
removed by physical processes such as adsorption [33,37]. Thus, elec­
tron transfer and highly reactive Fe mineral production in the system 
can be enhanced by microbubbles, favorably contributing to C1 
removal. The removal of C2 in the MFC system could be attributed to the 
improved charge effects.
The relevant optical parameters of biogas slurry were further used to 
assess the contribution of different types of DOM. The specific UV 
absorbance (SUVA) describes the aromatic content in humic substances, 
typically associated with electron-rich and light-absorbing moieties 
containing C = C and C = O double bonds [18]. The results (Fig. 2e) 
showed that the SUVA of the MFC system is significantly lower than the 
other systems (p < 0.05). The heightened generation of iron ions by the 
MFC system facilitated the elimination of aromatic substances as the C =
C and C = O can increase the sites for complex metal ion binding 
[16,33]. This phenomenon further contributed to the biochemistry in­
crease of biogas slurry [6]. The fluorescence index (FI) is used to identify 
the relative contribution of land-sourced and microbial-sourced DOM in 
C1. The MFC system exhibited a lower FI value (<1.4) than the CFC 
system, indicating that the degradation of microbial-sourced metabo­
lites contributes more to DOM removal. The biological index (BIX) in­
dicates the level of autotrophic productivity, implying heightened 
bioavailability with elevated values [18]. MFC and CFC systems showed 
higher BIX than MBs systems due to the higher removal ratio of C1. The 
freshness index (β:α) indicated that only the MFC system significantly 
differed from RBS (p < 0.05), suggesting more soluble compounds were 
produced during degradation.
As for the UV-active substances, UV 2D-COS was used to derive 
removal mechanisms in different systems (Fig. S10). The UV- 
synchronous spectra illustrate that more UV-active substances are 
removed in the presence of microbubbles [37]. UV-asynchronous 
spectra suggest that the reduction of benzenoid was more sensitive 
with microbubbles. Detailed discussion is available in the Text S14. PCA 
results showed that the explained variance of the samples separated in 
the first and second principal axes for each system was 76.4 % and 15.5 
%, respectively (Fig. 2f). Indicators representing DOM content (i.e., 
SUVA and TF) were clustered at the positive side of the first principal 
axis. Their narrow-angle relative to the first principal axis contributed to 
better sample separation. The sample points of the MFC system were 
distributed on the negative side of the first principal axis, indicating that 
MFC systems exhibited superior DOM removal than CFC and MBs sys­
tems. The indicators representing the autochthonous DOM (i.e., BIX and 
β: α) were clustered at the negative side of the first principal axis. Their 
positions in the load plot corresponded closely to the positions of the 
samples in the MFC system of the score plot, suggesting that the MFC 
system produces more soluble small molecule DOM.
3.3. High oxidizing properties accelerate electron transfer
The degradation efficiency of DOM was correlated with the electron 
transfer rate of Fe-C micro-electrolysis [15], so the effect of micro­
bubbles on the electron transfer rate in the MFC system was further 
investigated. The electron transfer rate can be reflected by the corrosion 
of Fe. Analysis via SEM revealed the corrosion of Fe on the surface of Fe- 
C particles. Compared to the raw Fe-C particles, the surface of Fe-C 
particles from both the MFC and CFC systems (Fig. 3) exhibited 
increased roughness and porosity, where the corrosion of Fe causes the 
creation of voids on the surface. Notably, the surface of Fe-C particles 
from MFC systems was covered by more tiny floc particles, indicating 
more pronounced corrosion of the Fe [39]. This phenomenon was 
attributed to microbubbles with extensive diffusion capability, pene­
trating the micropores of the Fe-C particles and intensifying the oxida­
tive dissolution of Fe. Previous studies have demonstrated that the 
dissolved Fe can form nanoparticles, promoting the formation of tiny 
floc [33]. Elemental distribution (Fig. 3) shows a higher quantity of Fe 
on the surface of Fe-C particles in the MFC system (14.91 %) compared 
to the CFC system (9.16 %), indicating that more dissolved iron ions are 
reabsorbed to the surface.
The electron transfer process at the anode consumes H+ causing an 
increase in pH. The pH value measured approximately 7.13 in the MFC

system after operation (Fig. 4a). The MFC system was more alkaline 
compared to the CFC system, confirming that the microbubbles accel­
erated the electron transfer rate in the system. Additionally, XRD 
demonstrated that peaks of Fe and FeO in Fe-C particles of the MFC 
system were lower than the CFC system (Fig. S12a). These results sug­

rate of microbubbles accelerates the oxidation of Fe(II) to Fe(III) and the 
subsequent formation of insoluble Fe minerals. Dissolved iron ions in the 
CFC system primarily exist as Fe(II) due to the acidic environment 
reducing the oxidation rate of Fe(II) [39]. This also theoretically ex­
plains the superior adsorption and coagulation capacities for pollutants

in the MFC system compared to the CFC system.
The generation of active species has a non-negligible contribution to 
electron transfer and DOM degradation. Microbubbles can generate •OH 
to induce the oxidative transformation of Fe and DOM [8]. Fig. 4b il­
lustrates minimal •OH formation in the CFC system. In contrast, •OH 
production increased over time in the MFC and MBs systems, indicating 
that the microbubbles can effectively promote •OH generation. The 
higher levels of •OH in the MFC system compared to the MBs system 
could be attributed to the presence of persistent free radicals (PFRs) in 
the carbon [27], which promotes •OH production [4]. Previous studies 
have also reported that Fe minerals are capable of reducing oxygen to 
produce •OH [21]. Additionally, Fe(IV) can degrade DOM. As shown in 
Fig. S12b, there is almost no formation of Fe(IV) in any system, indi­
cating the degradation of DOM by Fe(IV) can be neglected.
To reveal the impact of corrosion products and adsorbed particulate 
matter on electron transfer during Fe-C micro-electrolysis, the electro­
chemical properties of Fe-C particles were analyzed. The cyclic vol­
tammogram curve (Fig. 4d) illustrates that the double electric layer 
capacitance of the Fe-C particles in the MFC system is larger than that of 
the CFC system, implying that the microbubbles may facilitate the for­
mation of additional electrochemical active sites. The Nyquist plots of 
electrochemical impedance spectroscopy (EIS) are shown in Fig. 4e. 
Based on the fitting results (Fig. 4f), the charge transfer resistance (Rct) 
of Fe-C particles in the MFC system (11.8 O) is lower compared to both 
the raw Fe-C particles (16.2 O) and CFC system (14.1 O), which is 
consistent with previous studies [18]. Rapid micro-electrolytic reactions 
and corrosion occurred in the MFC system with the assistance of 
microbubbles, and the corrosion products formed on the surface accel­
erated the interfacial charge transfer between the solution and the Fe-C 
particles. The Warburg impedance (W1) of the Fe-C particles in the MFC 
system (225.4 O) is also lower than that of both raw Fe-C particles 
(436.4 O) and the CFC system (363.9 O). This suggests a reduced 
diffusion resistance of ions in the solution within the voids of the Fe-C 
particles in the MFC system, enhancing the reaction rate. This could 
be attributed to microbubbles potentially fully oxidizing the iron within 
these voids and subsequently enhancing ion diffusion.
3.4. DOM removal by formation of stable structures in flocs
Flocs formation plays a key role in DOM removal. Due to rapid 
electron transfer leading to the formation of more Fe (hydr)oxides, a 
higher quantity of flocs (Fig. 5a) was formed in the MFC system (2907.4 
mg/L) compared to the CFC system (1387.1 mg/L). Nearly all generated 
Fe in the MFC system was bound within the flocs, whereas 35.0 mg/L of 
iron ions remained in the supernatant of the CFC system (Fig. 5b). Faster 
electron transfer and settling rates result in flocs with higher Fe content 
in MFC systems compared to CFC systems (Fig. 5c). This implies that the 
formation of additional Fe (hydr)oxides and stable DOM binding sites in 
the MFC system facilitated the simultaneous removal of Fe and DOM.
To reveal the binding modes of DOM in flocs, the organic functional 
groups within the flocs were analyzed. Fourier Transform Infrared 
Spectroscopy (FTIR) results (Fig. 5e) showed the binding modes of DOM 
in flocs. The peak at 3412 cm−1 arises from the −
OH vibration, repre­
senting the contribution of absorbed water and organic hydroxyl groups 
[33]. 2927 cm−1 corresponds to the asymmetric (νC-H asym) stretch of 
the aliphatic compound [4]. Vibration at 1644 cm−1 arises from the 
carbonyl group (C = O) of aromatic rings in the aromatic compound 
[43], while 1545 and 1385 cm−1 were assigned to asymmetric (νC-O 
asym) and symmetric (νC-O sym) stretching motions of the adsorbed 
carboxyl group, respectively [34]. The band at 1038 and 470 cm−1 was 
identified as the characteristic vibration of C-O and Fe-O lattice 
stretching modes, respectively [41]. Some of the peaks of the flocs in the 
MFC system showed changes compared to the CFC system, indicating 
possible differences in the type and abundance of DOM bound by the 
flocs. Furthermore, SR-FTIR analysis was conducted to assess the dis­
tribution of organic functional groups within the flocs, confirming 
substantial differences between the two systems (Fig. 5f). Specifically, 
the alterations in C = O (1644 cm−1), νC-O sym (1385 cm−1), and C-O 
(1038 cm−1) indicated increased interactions of carboxyl and carbonyl 
groups with edges of flocs [34], probably because microbubbles increase 
the positive surface charge of the Fe (hydr)oxides. Furthermore, the 
band change at 1038 cm−1 was the most pronounced and shifted to the 
higher frequency, indicating that the flocs were mainly combined with 
DOM through inner-sphere adsorption, possibly the carbonyl group in 
the DOM forms a covalent bond with the Fe (hydr)oxides [33].

The flocs on the composition and proportion of elements based on X- 
ray photoelectron spectroscopy (XPS) further verified the positive ef­
fects of microbubbles on DOM binding modes. Peaks corresponding to 
Fe2p, O1s, C1s, and P2p were observed in flocs (Fig. S13a). The high- 
resolution C1s spectra (Fig. 5d) showed peaks concentrated around 
284.8, 286.3, and 288.2 eV, representing C–C/C–H bonds in hydrocar­
bon compounds, C–O–C/C–O bonds in carbonyl groups, and O–C=O/ 
O–C–O bonds in carboxyl-containing substances, respectively [33]. The 
primary forms of organic matter in flocs were aromatic carbon, α-car­
bon, and carboxyl carbon. The characteristic peaks of both C–O–C/C–O 
and O–C=O/O–C–O bonds exhibited a shift toward higher binding en­
ergy in the MFC system compared to the CFC system. This phenomenon 
results from the interaction between Fe minerals and organic matter, 
altering the electrostatic potential field of the core electrons of the C 
atom [16]. The proportion of α-carbon and carboxyl carbon in the MFC 
system exceeded that in the CFC system. This suggests that more organic 
matters were bound to flocs through carboxyl and carbonyl groups via 
electrostatic interactions, aligning with FTIR results. Studies have 
shown that the carboxyl group on DOM is partially ligand-complex with 
the –OH groups on Fe (hydr)oxides to form inner-sphere complexation 
[33]. The Fe2p spectra of samples are shown in Fig. S13b. The higher Fe 
(III) content in the CFC system than in the MFC system suggests that the 
microbubbles possessed a greater oxidizing capacity, enhancing the 
binding capability of flocs with organic matter. Furthermore, the Fe/C 
ratio (Fig. 5c) implies that the ability of unit Fe atoms to bind C atoms is 
higher in the MFC system (0.92) than CFC system (0.42).
3.5. Accelerated coagulation by the accumulation of ferrihydrite
The amorphous Fe mineral (e.g., ferrihydrite) in flocs hinders further 
research by conventional means. To further understand the effect of floc 
structure on coagulation, the mineral structure and coordination envi­
ronment of Fe within flocs were examined using EXAFS. Linear combi­
nation fitting (LCF) showed that the flocs were predominantly 
ferrihydrite, accounting for 84.8 % and 66.3 % of the MFC and CFC 
system, respectively, the rest were lepidocrocite and maghemite. This 
indicates that the microbubbles impede the transformation of ferrihy­
drite to highly crystalline minerals. The Wavelet transform (WT) ana­
lyses of reference minerals and floc structures are shown in Fig. 6 and 
Fig. S14. The signals at R = 1.46 Å and R = 2.57 Å were observed in two 
samples, indicating coordination bonds in the first and second shell 
layers, respectively. The peak positions of the coordination bonds were 
close to the reference minerals, meaning that the coordination bonds in 
the first and second shell layers are dominated by Fe-O and Fe-Fe paths,

The local coordination environment of Fe in flocs was explored by 
shell-fit analyses of k3-weighted Fe K-edge EXAFS spectra. Two Fe-O 
paths were required to accurately model the first O shell with the 
same Debye-Waller parameters (σ2). The Fe-O1 (1.93 Å) and Fe-O2 
(2.00 Å) paths represent FeO4 tetrahedra and FeO6 octahedra, respec­
tively [22]. In subsequent fits extended to 4.0 Å (R+△R), the σ2 of Fe-O 
paths were fixed to reduce the variables. The final fit model contained 
three additional Fe-Fe paths representative of edge- (Fe-Fe1), double 
corner- (Fe-Fe2), and single corner-sharing Fe (Fe-Fe3) [28].
The final model fits are illustrated in Fig. 6 and the corresponding 
EXAFS parameters are summarized in Table S7. For the first shell, the 
coordination numbers of Fe-O1 and Fe-O2 are 2.0 and 2.4 in the MFC 
system and 2.3 and 2.9 in the CFC system, respectively. This result 
suggests that more proportional FeO4 tetrahedra were formed in the 
MFC system (45.5 %), leading to a decrease degeneracy (N) sum of the 
Fe-O paths. Additionally, the reduced Fe-O distance distributions lead to 
significant octahedral distortions, resulting in phase-canceling interfer­
ence of the individual Fe-O scattered waves [28]. For the iron shells, the 
flocs in the CFC and MFC systems have the same number of Fe1 atoms. 
The number of Fe2 atoms in the flocs of the MFC system is lower than 
that of the CFC system. Surface negatively charged microbubbles can 
interact with Fe(III) [8]. The continuous perturbation of microbubbles 
might disrupt the crystal structure and inhibit the double corner coor­

might inhibit further transformation of ferrihydrite. The accumulation 
of ferrihydrite could readily adsorb DOM in the biogas slurry, due to its 
remarkable sorption capacity and high surface area [5]. With the 
introduction of microbubbles, the oxidation rate of Fe was accelerated, 
resulting in faster precipitation. Consequently, the contribution of single 
corner-sharing Fe increased rapidly, which favors the formation of more 
single corner-sharing dimers. Although lepidocrocite has a single-corner

3.6. Specific pollutant removal improves microalgae cultivation
The treated biogas slurry of all three systems promoted the growth of 
microalgae compared to RBS (Fig. 7a). To regulate the nutrient ratios, 
8.4 mg/L phosphate (TAP medium phosphate solution) was further 
supplemented to the biogas slurry (NH4
+-N/PO4
3--P = 14:1 after supple­
mentation). The biomass of the MFC system increased by 42.7 % and 
101.1 % compared to the CFC and MBs systems, respectively, after 10- 
fold dilution of the biogas slurry (Fig. 7b). This suggests that the MFC 
system greatly improves the microalgae growth environment by 
reducing turbidity and removing microalgal stressors (e.g., humic-like 
substances, aromatic compounds, and residual iron ions) from the 
biogas slurry.
The removal of microalgal stressors from biogas slurry in different 
systems was reflected by the oxidative stress reactions in microalgae 
cells (Fig. 7d). The increase in these biomarkers implies that microalgae 
cells may be subjected to oxidative stress damage. Previous studies 
showed that high concentrations of humic acid can penetrate microalgae 
cells, damage cell membranes, and thereby cause oxidative stress [40]. 
After pretreatment, the oxidative damage of microalgae cells was alle­
viated, especially in the MFC system with the lowest reactive oxygen 
species (ROS), malondialdehyde (MDA), and catalase (CAT) levels. This 
indicates that the reduction of harmful substances such as humic acid in 
biogas slurry after pretreatment can effectively improve the growth of 
microalgae. Furthermore, hydrophilic functional groups (e.g., carboxyl 
groups) in aromatic compounds can bind with hydroxyl groups in 
extracellular polymeric substances (EPS) via H-bonds [3], which can 
cause oxidative stress. Section 3.3 has demonstrated that the carboxyl 
group in the biogas slurry is involved in the binding of flocs and Fe 
minerals and can be effectively removed. Furthermore, ROS can also be 
generated due to abiotic stress from exposure to metal ions. In the CFC 
system, the concentration of remaining iron ions in the supernatant 
reached 35.0 mg/L, surpassing the threshold conducive to microalgae 
growth, potentially inducing oxidative stress to a certain extent.
Additionally, oxidative damage might adversely affect microalgae 
photosynthesis. The following biophysical parameters (Fig. 7c) were 
determined: the maximum quantum yield (Fm) and conversion effi­
ciency (Fv/Fm) of primary photochemistry; specific energy flux per re­
action center (RC), including absorption energy (ABS/RC), electron 
transport energy (ETo/RC), trapping energy (TRo/RC); performance 
index (Pi_Abs) of light energy absorption. The values of Fv/Fm, Fm, and 
Pi_Abs generally decreased with increasing levels of oxidative stress, 
whereas the values of TRo/RC, ETo/RC, and ABS/RC were positively 
correlated with oxidative stress levels. In addition to the reduced 
oxidative stress, the MFC system greatly reduces the turbidity of the 
biogas slurry and increases the light transmittance, thereby significantly 
improving photosynthetic performance. The results indicate that the 
pretreatment of the biogas slurry increased the light conversion effi­
ciency in the photochemical reaction center and the energy absorption 
parameter. Compared with the RBS (0.455), the Fv/Fm values in the 
MFC (0.556), CFC (0.521), and MBs (0.507) systems were increased by 
22.2 %, 14.5 %, and 11.4 %, respectively, while the Pi_Abs values were 
increased by 111.1 %, 81.5 %, and 50.0 %, respectively. Microalgal 
stressors in the biogas slurry interfered with enzyme activity and 
photosynthesis on chloroplasts, leading to the down-regulation of major 
proteins (PsbB, PsbC, and PsbD). Furthermore, ROS generation could 
disrupt the chloroplast structure and membrane lipid peroxidation ho­
meostasis, ultimately restricting photosynthetic electron transport [12]. 
Consequently, the absorption (ABS/RC), transfer (ETo/RC), and dissi­
pate (DI0/RC) energy per RC increased due to the inactivation of some 
RCs [17].
The nutrient utilization in the biogas slurry from the MFC system by 
microalgae was further investigated. The NH4
+-N concentration 
decreased to 1.61 mg/L on day 7 with a removal rate of 98.58 % 
(Fig. 7e). Phosphate concentration in the supernatant was below the 
detectable limit level after day 5 (Fig. 7f). The decrease in phosphate 
concentration did not significantly affect the growth rate of microalgae. 
Microalgae can absorb excess phosphate, storing it within cells for 
growth metabolism and energy synthesis in phosphate-deficient 
external environments. Correspondingly, the biomass of microalgae 
cultured in the biogas slurry increased to 1.47 g/L after 7 days (Fig. 7h). 
Interestingly, the concentration of TOC increased from an initial 17.96 
mg/L to 53.12 mg/L (Fig. 7g), which is contrary to the results in some 
studies [42]. It might be attributed to microalgae converting fixed 
inorganic carbon into organic carbon during photosynthesis, subse­
quently releasing converted organic carbon into the system as extra­
cellular secretions. Therefore, coupling the MFC system with microalgae 
cultivation can achieve efficient utilization of nitrogen and phosphorus 
nutrients in the biogas slurry and promote the conversion and storage of 
CO2 to organic carbon.
3.7. MFC-driven microalgae-based biogas slurry treatment mechanism
Based on the above proof-of-concept, we propose the mechanism for 
MFC-driven oxidative synergistic self-accelerating coagulation to 
improve microalgae-based biogas slurry treatment (Fig. 8). Micro­
bubbles increase oxygen mass transfer and electron transfer rates to 
optimize the efficiency of Fe-C micro-electrolysis. Meanwhile, the 
presence of PFRs in Fe-C particles increased the amount of •OH pro­
duced during microbubble collapse [9,27], further accelerating the 
degradation of pollutants and the generation of Fe(III). The acceleration 
of the micro-electrolysis process results in an alkaline environment in 
the system, which is conducive to the production of ferrihydrite with 
high adsorption properties [30]. Surface negatively charged micro­
bubbles can interact with Fe(III) [8]. Therefore, the continuous pertur­
bation of microbubbles inhibits the transformation of hydrotalcite to a 
highly crystalline mineral, which leads to the accumulation of hydro­
talcite and self-accelerated coagulation. Subsequently, the specific types 
of DOM (e.g., carboxyl groups) in the biogas slurry were more easily 
removed by forming a more stable structure in the flocs, thereby 
reducing the coercive effects on microalgae of binding to functional 
groups in the EPS [3]. In addition, particulate matter was removed by 
coagulation, improving the light utilization of microalgae. Efficient 
removal of these stressors reduced oxidative stress in microalgae and 
increased the maximum quantum yield of the photosynthetic system. 
Consequently, nutrients such as nitrogen and phosphorus in the biogas 
slurry are efficiently utilized by microalgae, and microalgae biomass is 
notably increased.
4. Conclusions
This study presented a novel MFC system for biogas slurry pre­
treatment, improving its suitability for microalgae cultivation, as well as 
breaking through the roadblocks of conventional wastewater resource 
utilization. The MFC system not only overcame the limitation of electron 
transfer efficiency in the conventional Fe-C treatment system but also 
shifted the focus of Fe-C micro-electrolysis research to the coagulation- 
driven removal of pollutants. The results demonstrated that micro­
bubbles achieved efficient removal of DOM by accelerating the

oxidation and coagulation processes, revealing the mechanism of self- 
accelerating coagulation during Fe-C micro-electrolysis. These findings 
have critical implications for the application of Fe-C treatment systems 
in water treatment and the Fe cycle in nature. In addition, the response 
of parameters such as microalgae oxidative stress and photosynthetic 
activity to the removal of specific types of DOM in complex systems of 
biogas slurry was investigated. This provides a reference for the selective 
removal of biotic stressors in future bioremediation technology studies. 
Compared with the CFC system, the MFC system can transfer most of the 
iron ions in the solution to the floc due to better flocculation charac­
teristics, reducing the risk of secondary contamination of dissolved iron 
ions. Although phosphate transfer to the flocs as strengite or vivianite 
during the Fe-C micro-electrolysis may diminish the available amount in 
the supernatant for microalgae growth, subsequent pH adjustments 
could release these compounds for further utilization. Therefore, 
coupling the MFC system with microalgae cultivation can achieve effi­
cient utilization of nutrients in the biogas slurry and promote CO2 
sequestration. Furthermore, the MFC system has great potential for 
scaling up due to ease of operation and low retrofit costs. Previous 
studies have also indicated that in industrial-scale implementations, 
microbubbles reduce energy consumption through improved efficiency, 
lowering total costs by 40 % over a decade [8]. Overall, this study not 
only inspires future creativity and innovation in the Fe cycle and 
bioremediation technologies of wastewater treatment but also provides 
a promising process with great potential for supporting the transition to 
sustainable water treatment.
